blocks.x: For those who want their animated sheep comedy even cozier than The Sheep Detectives or those looking for cartoons whose silent-movie bona fides run even deeper than Coyote Vs. Acme, Aardman Animations preempts Halloween season with the charming Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom. Where Shaun’s previous film, Farmageddon, threw all things sci-fi at the rascally wooly, The Beast Of Mossy Bottom does the same for classic horror. Filled with silly Universal Monsters-spanning imagery and nary a word of spoken dialogue, the ultra-accessible stop-motion feature provides a kid-friendly on-ramp to another genre while mostly eschewing the more obnoxious trends of modern feature animation. It’s simple, soft, and warm, like a stuffed-animal version of a horror movie: inoffensive and, to a select group of kids, likely essential.

With that innocuous approach comes the inevitable comparison that Aardman’s best work (the Wallace & Gromit shorts and feature film) puts its rounded Plasticine into sharper scenarios. Still, those with young children will likely find The Beast Of Mossy Bottom a far easier sell, when introducing their kids to the wide world of spooky cinema, than Abbott And Costello Meet Frankenstein. There’s a shared sense of doofy festive slapstick between the two, but now the mad-scientist laboratory—a hand-molded amusement park of spiraling glassware and weird gadgets—is staffed by farm animals rather than studio day players. This means that when Shaun and his flock turn to (mad) science in order to re-grow their patch of pumpkins in the wake of disaster, the ensuing chaos they wreak upon The Farmer is a lot more cute.

The Beast Of Mossy Bottom‘s spin on a Wolf Man-like plot will be familiar to those who’ve seen a monster movie or two, or even those who’ve seen holiday episodes of cartoon sitcoms: The balding Farmer gets his mitts on some of the quick-grow formula Shaun concocts and believes it meant for his hairline; after animals and human alike put it to use, the pumpkins get huge and a hirsute beast stalks around their farm. As the clever animals, hapless Farmer, and competent Vet (whom The Farmer has a crush on) try to solve this extremely furry problem through grunts, sighs, and Simlish-style murmuring—not to mention the requisite number of Aardman-approved Rube Goldberg machines—the spooky references are doled out with the everything-must-go speed of a Spirit Halloween on November 1st.

The horror is mainly contained in aesthetic pastiche—in pumpkin-gut gore, harmless cuckoo-clock jump scares, enjoyably dramatic deep-hued giallo lighting, and references ranging from Psycho to Ghostbusters—dressing the traditional Aardman-style comedy up in an endearing costume. There are still the lightly zany chases, but now they race across foggy docks, flee from angry mobs wielding toy pitchforks, and culminate at climactic windmills. There are still the charmingly detailed sight gags, but now they involve things like the empty fingers of Shaun’s Frankensteinian rubber gloves flapping around because he’s got hooves shoved into them. Directors Steve Cox and Matthew Walker keep the timing for both tight, allowing enough time for a reaction to the candy-corny gags while maintaining a quick enough pace that the film never feels like the last stretch of the cul-de-sac after a long night of trick-or-treating.

The story’s simplicity, the humor’s breeziness, and the latent power of the genre imagery (especially when translated through the tactile sculptural materials) are only helped by the silent-movie ethos pervading all things Shaun. Even Natalie Holt’s score harkens back to the era, cute and representative of the onscreen action without being overbearing. The same cannot be said for the needledrops, which The Beast Of Mossy Bottom is as bad at as its more crass American contemporaries. But if getting throwbacks to James Whale movies means gritting through the stop-motion cast dancing to a rap song, that’s an even trade. As a standalone comedy, The Beast Of Mossy Bottom is too mild to be a crossover favorite threatening to entertain parents as much as their offspring. As a sly introduction to all things classic horror, though, it’s a solid holiday gateway for (very) young cinephiles.
Starring: Justin Fletcher, John Sparkes, Kate Harbour
